subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 5 periods = 200 minutes
Total: 5 periods · 3h 20min

periods.activity_title: Building and Breaking: Adding and Subtracting with Blocks

tasks_in_class.description: Complete snake/caterpillar chains: Add 2 from 334; Add 5 from 375; Subtract 5 from 387.
Draw box diagrams and use HTO blocks or number line to solve: (1) 456−63; (2) 309+80; (3) 270−36.
Write word problems for two given box diagrams (234 boys +156 girls; 356 books −138 books) and solve them using pictures as context clues.

time_bands.activity: Open with p.150 ("Complete snake/caterpillar chains: Add 2 from 334...."). Students work in pairs on the warm-up chains, calling out answers aloud while the teacher models the first chain on the board using HTO headings, showing that adding ones keeps the hundreds digit unchanged.

Introduce the Kishan nursery story from the 3-digit addition with Dienes blocks section. Using actual Dienes blocks (or drawn squares, sticks, dots on the board), model combining 364 + 52: lay out hundreds, tens, and ones; combine tens; exchange 10 tens for 1 hundred where needed. Then move to subtraction: tell the sapling-packing story from the 3-digit subtraction with regrouping section and model 230 − 75 step by step in an HTO table on the board, making each exchange visible. Students follow along with their own blocks or draw the exchange on paper.

Students tackle Let us Do Q1–3, p.154 ("Draw box diagrams and use HTO blocks or number line to solve...."). Each student draws the box diagram first, then solves using either blocks or a number-line strategy. The teacher circulates, checking that the box diagram is drawn before any calculation begins.

Let us Do, p.154 ("Write word problems for two given box diagrams...."). Students read the two given diagrams and write a short sentence naming what the numbers represent, then solve. A quick share of one story from the class closes the unit.

periods.teacher_notes: Students working with 3-digit addition and subtraction for the first time often forget to regroup: they write the ones digit of a two-digit ones-sum without carrying the ten, or subtract the smaller digit from the larger regardless of position. Ensure each child draws the HTO box before computing; the physical act of labelling the columns holds place value in view. For the word-problem task, accept any sensible real-world context — the goal is for students to connect a box diagram to a story, not to produce a formally worded problem.
materials: Dienes blocks (hundreds flats, tens rods, ones cubes) or home-made paper cut-outs
Squared paper or HTO table printed sheet

periods.activity_title: Grid Walks and Chain Drills: Seeing Place Value Move

tasks_in_class.description: Extend two chains: Add 100 repeatedly from 269; Add 10 repeatedly from 269; Add 1 repeatedly from 269; repeat for 454.

time_bands.activity: Distribute the 451–530 number grid (or have students open to p.155). Ask the class: 'When you add 10 to a number, which row do you move to — the one above or below?' Students point and discuss in pairs before any calculations begin.

p.155 ("Use the 451–530 grid to solve and colour answers...."). Students locate 456 on the grid, then move right/down to add, left/up to subtract, colouring each answer in a chosen colour. After completing all six calculations, pairs compare grids and discuss: 'What pattern do you see in the coloured squares?' The teacher draws out observations — adding 10 always moves one row down, adding 1 moves one cell right — making the positional structure of the number grid explicit.

Do as directed, p.156 ("Extend two chains: Add 100 repeatedly from 269...."). Students extend all three sub-chains for 269 (add 100, add 10, add 1) and repeat for 454. After filling the chains, the teacher asks: 'When you added 100 each time, which digit changed? When you added 1, which digit changed?' Students circle the changing digit in each step, arriving inductively at the rule about which place-value column responds to each operation.

Brief class discussion: a student reads out one completed chain aloud; the class says together which digit changed. The Jadupur barter story from the place-value patterns section is read aloud, connecting the abstract digit-change observation to the real-world give-and-take context.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently confuse the direction of grid movement: they add 10 by moving right (adding 1 ten cells) rather than down one row. On the HTO chain task, a common error is changing all three digits when adding 100, rather than only the hundreds digit. Ask students to cover the tens and ones with a finger and watch only the hundreds column change — this physical gesture reinforces which column the operation touches.
materials: 451–530 number grid (one per student, printed or from textbook p.155)
Coloured pencils (at least two colours per student)

section_titles: Indian currency: notes, coins, and equivalence
periods.activity_title: Notes and Coins: Making the Same Amount Many Ways

tasks_in_class.description: Circle the item that costs more: a milk bottle or a pomegranate, when both are bought for ₹100.
Match notes and coins in two columns that have the same total values.
Use given notes and coins to buy items priced ₹55, ₹30, ₹28, ₹20; find at least two ways of making each amount.
Draw as many ₹100 notes as equal one ₹500 note; state how many ₹100 notes = ₹500; name things you can buy with ₹500.

time_bands.activity: Spread cut-out or play currency notes (₹10, ₹20, ₹50, ₹100) on each desk-group. Ask: 'If you had one ₹100 note, what could you buy — a milk bottle or a pomegranate?' Students discuss and then open to p.157 ("Circle the item that costs more...."), marking their answer and explaining their reasoning to a partner.

p.158 ("Match notes and coins in two columns that have the same total values."). Students add up each group in the left column, then each group in the right column, and draw lines between equal totals. The teacher asks after each match: 'How did you know these were equal?' This draws out the idea that the same total can look different when different denominations are used.

p.159 ("Use given notes and coins to buy items priced ₹55, ₹30, ₹28, ₹20...."). Groups of three students use their play notes and coins to physically 'pay' for each item in at least two different ways, arranging the notes on the desk before recording. The teacher visits each group and asks: 'Can you find a third way for ₹28?' to push toward flexibility.

p.159 ("Draw as many ₹100 notes as equal one ₹500 note...."). Students draw the five ₹100 notes, write the equivalence statement, and name two or three things they think cost around ₹500. A quick share closes the unit: the teacher records a few student suggestions on the board to anchor the face-value reasoning concretely.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often confuse the face value of a note with the number of notes — they may say 'five notes is more than one note' rather than comparing totals. The matching task on p.158 is the key corrective: insist students compute the total of each group rather than counting pieces. For the multi-way payment task, encourage students who finish quickly to find a third combination for each price — this extends the reasoning without introducing new content.
materials: Play currency notes and coins (₹10, ₹20, ₹50, ₹100, ₹500 cut-outs or printed play money)

periods.activity_title: Peter Uncle's Shop: Money Word Problems and Estimation

tasks_in_class.description: Solve using box diagrams and notes or number line: (1) ₹650+₹250; (2) ₹500−₹209; (3) ₹150+₹100×4 weeks; (4) ₹250+₹125+₹350.
Estimate 7 expressions to the nearest hundred and discuss: 156+34, 125−15, 105+195, 205+215, 500−395, 765−567, 505+405.

time_bands.activity: Read aloud the Peter uncle shop scenario from the addition and subtraction with money section. Work through the modelled example ₹756 − ₹465 on the board using the pictorial note-layout method: draw note images grouped into hundreds, tens, and ones strips, cross out what is taken away, count what remains. Students copy the layout and say the result.

Let us Do Q1–4, p.161–162 ("Solve using box diagrams and notes or number line...."). Students draw a box diagram for each problem before writing any calculation. Q3 (₹150 saved each week for 4 weeks) is worked through together first — the teacher models repeated addition on the number line — before students attempt Q4 independently. The teacher circulates, checking that regrouping with hundreds is recorded correctly in the HTO layout.

p.162 ("Estimate 7 expressions to the nearest hundred and discuss...."). The teacher demonstrates rounding 156 to 200 (nearest hundred) and 34 to 0, giving an estimate of 200. Students work through the remaining six expressions individually, rounding each addend or subtrahend first, then adding or subtracting the rounded values. Pairs compare estimates and discuss any that gave surprising results.

Quick oral round: the teacher reads one expression; students call out their estimate and a one-word reason ('round up' or 'round down'). This closes the unit on the distinction between an exact answer and a reasonable estimate.

periods.teacher_notes: A frequent error in multi-step money problems is treating repeated addition as multiplication before the concept is formally introduced — students may write '4 × ₹150' without a framework for it. Redirect them to draw four ₹150 boxes and add in two steps: ₹150 + ₹150 = ₹300, then ₹300 + ₹300 = ₹600, keeping the box diagram as the scaffold. In the estimation task, students often round 156 to 100 rather than 200; establish the rule that 50 and above rounds to the next hundred before the task begins.
materials: Play currency notes (₹100, ₹50, ₹10, ₹1 coins or cut-outs)
HTO table printed sheet or squared paper

section_titles: Number card game and computation drill
periods.activity_title: Think First, Then Play: Mental Maths and the Card Game

tasks_in_class.description: Compare 5 pairs of expressions without calculating; circle the one that is more in each pair.
Fill in boxes in the number web connecting 120 and 130 via +3/−3/+7/−7 operations, extending to 156 and 175.
Make cards 0–5; form two 3-digit numbers; add and subtract them; rearrange for biggest sum and smallest difference; compare with friends.

time_bands.activity: p.163 ("Compare 5 pairs of expressions without calculating...."). Students read each pair silently, then circle their choice — no pencil calculation allowed. After all five, the teacher asks: 'How did you decide? What did you look at?' Students articulate which digit (tens or ones) tipped the comparison, surfacing the mental-arithmetic strategy.

p.163 ("Find which pairs among 516+100, 400+15, 615−200, 450−50, 350+50, 816−200 are equal."). Students compute each expression mentally or with minimal jottings, list the results, and draw lines between equal ones. Class confirms answers together. Then p.163 ("Fill in boxes in the number web....") — students work individually on the +3/−3/+7/−7 web, checking that each path from a node gives the correct neighbour.

p.164 ("Make cards 0–5; form two 3-digit numbers; add and subtract them...."). Each student writes digits 0–5 on small paper squares. Working in pairs, they arrange six cards into two 3-digit numbers, compute the sum and difference, then rearrange to find the arrangement giving the biggest sum. Partners compare results and discuss: 'Why does putting the largest digits in the hundreds place give the biggest sum?' This brings place-value reasoning from earlier in the chapter to bear on an open strategic question.

Let us Do (a)–(f), p.164 ("Solve equations: (a) 265+9, (b) 405+56...."). Students work through all six equations independently, showing working in an HTO layout. The teacher scans quickly, noting which students struggle with (d) 600−82 (two exchanges needed from zero tens) and (f) 653−356 (regrouping across both columns) for targeted follow-up.

periods.teacher_notes: The mental comparison task is undermined if students are allowed to calculate — enforce no-pencil for that task so the reasoning is genuinely comparative rather than computational. In the card game, students sometimes place larger digits in the ones column by accident; ask them to predict before computing and then check: 'Did the bigger hundreds digit give the bigger sum?' For 600 − 82, remind students who are stuck that they can exchange the one hundred for 10 tens, then exchange one ten for 10 ones, working the HTO table one column at a time.
materials: Small paper squares or index cards (six per student, labelled 0–5)

items.section_title: Number card game and computation drill
items.prompt: Write the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 on five small paper squares. Use all five cards to make two 3-digit numbers (one number uses 3 cards, the other uses 2 cards — place a 0 in the empty hundreds place of the 2-card number if needed). Add your two numbers. Now rearrange the same cards to make two new 3-digit numbers whose sum is as large as possible. Write both arrangements and their sums. Which arrangement gives the bigger sum?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Placing the largest digits in the hundreds places gives the biggest sum. For example, 5, 4, 3 form 543 and 2, 1 (with 0 in hundreds) form 021 — but rearranging so the two largest digits head each number (e.g. 531 + 420 = 951 or 532 + 410 = 942) yields a larger total than placing small digits in the hundreds. The arrangement 543 + 210 = 753 is smaller than 531 + 420 = 951, showing the hundreds place drives the sum.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Place the two largest available digits in the hundreds positions of the two numbers to maximise the sum.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student first just add any two numbers they make; stretch: ask them to also find the arrangement that gives the smallest possible sum.

exercise.description: Make cards 0–5; form two 3-digit numbers; add and subtract them; rearrange for biggest sum and smallest difference; compare with friends.

items.prompt: A library has 248 story books and 95 picture books. Ravi says: 'The total is the same as 248 + 95.' Meena draws a box diagram with the two numbers and writes 248 in one box and 95 in another. She says the answer is more than 300. Is Meena right? Write how you know without doing the full addition.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Meena is right. 248 is close to 250 and 95 is close to 100; 250 + 100 = 350, which is more than 300. So the total must be more than 300.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Round each number to the nearest ten or hundred and add the rounded values to compare with 300.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to draw the box diagram and write both numbers inside, then count on from 248 by tens; stretch: ask what the total would be closer to — 300, 350, or 400 — and why.

exercise.description: Write word problems for two given box diagrams (234 boys +156 girls; 356 books −138 books) and solve them using pictures as context clues.

items.section_title: Indian currency: notes, coins, and equivalence
items.prompt: Priya has two ₹50 notes and three ₹10 coins. Arjun has one ₹100 note and one ₹20 note. Who has more money, and by how much?

options.label: A
options.text: Arjun has more; he has ₹10 extra.

options.label: B
options.text: Priya has more; she has ₹10 extra.

options.label: C
options.text: Priya has more; she has ₹30 extra.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Priya: ₹50 + ₹50 + ₹10 + ₹10 + ₹10 = ₹130. Arjun: ₹100 + ₹20 = ₹120. Priya has ₹130 − ₹120 = ₹10 more. Wait — rechecking: Priya has 2×50 + 3×10 = 100 + 30 = ₹130; Arjun has 100 + 20 = ₹120; difference = ₹10. The correct answer is Priya has more by ₹10.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add up the total for each person separately, then subtract the smaller total from the larger.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Student added both sets together rather than comparing them, or made an arithmetic error that equalised the two totals.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student computed Priya's total as ₹120 (forgetting one ₹10 coin) and Arjun's correctly as ₹120, or swapped the two totals.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student added all five of Priya's notes/coins as if each ₹50 note were ₹50+₹10 rather than computing correctly.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student lay out play notes and count each person's pile; stretch: ask what single note Arjun would need to add to match or beat Priya.

exercise.description: Match notes and coins in two columns that have the same total values.

items.section_title: Indian currency: notes, coins, and equivalence
items.prompt: Kiran has one ₹500 note. He wants to share it equally with his four friends so that each person (including himself) gets the same amount. How many ₹100 notes will each person get? Draw the ₹100 notes that equal ₹500, and then share them out.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Five ₹100 notes equal one ₹500 note. Five people sharing five ₹100 notes equally means each person gets one ₹100 note.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Draw five ₹100 notes (since 5 × ₹100 = ₹500), then distribute one to each of the five people.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student draw and count the ₹100 notes first before thinking about sharing; stretch: ask how much each person would get if Kiran had two ₹500 notes to share among five people.

exercise.description: Draw as many ₹100 notes as equal one ₹500 note; state how many ₹100 notes = ₹500; name things you can buy with ₹500.

items.prompt: Estimate 765 − 567 to the nearest hundred. Which of the following is the best estimate?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 765 rounds to 800; 567 rounds to 600. 800 − 600 = 200. However, a closer rounding: 765 rounds to 800 and 567 rounds to 600, giving 200. Re-examining: nearest hundred for 765 is 800, for 567 is 600; 800−600 = 200. The best estimate is 200.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Round each number to the nearest hundred, then subtract the rounded values.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student rounded both numbers down to 700 and 500, giving 200 — same result — or made a subtraction error after correct rounding.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student rounded 765 up to 800 but rounded 567 down to 500, giving 300 — an error in identifying the nearer hundred for 567.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student subtracted the rounded numbers in the wrong order or confused rounding with truncating to zero.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write the two numbers and draw a number line showing the nearest hundreds on either side; stretch: ask the student to also compute the exact answer and compare it with the estimate.

exercise.description: Estimate 7 expressions to the nearest hundred and discuss: 156+34, 125−15, 105+195, 205+215, 500−395, 765−567, 505+405.

items.prompt: Without calculating the exact answers, which expression gives a larger result?

options.label: D
options.text: It is not possible to tell without calculating.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 452 + 50 is larger because 50 is greater than 30; adding a larger number to the same starting number always gives a larger result.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare the numbers being added to the same starting value — the larger addend produces the larger sum.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student may have confused the addends or read the tens digits incorrectly.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student did not notice the difference between 30 and 50, treating both tens digits as equivalent.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student lacks confidence in mental comparison and believes calculation is always needed to compare.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to place both expressions on a number line starting at 452 and jump 30 steps vs 50 steps; stretch: ask the student to write their own pair of expressions where one is clearly larger without calculating.

exercise.description: Compare 5 pairs of expressions without calculating; circle the one that is more in each pair.

items.prompt: Look at these six expressions: 516 + 100, 400 + 15, 615 − 200, 450 − 50, 350 + 50, 816 − 200. Find two pairs of expressions that give the same answer. Write the pairs and their common value.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 516 + 100 = 616 and 816 − 200 = 616 (pair 1, common value 616). 400 + 15 = 415 and 615 − 200 = 415 (pair 2, common value 415). Also 450 − 50 = 400 and 350 + 50 = 400 (pair 3, common value 400).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compute each expression, then group those with the same result.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student compute all six values and write them in a list before hunting for matches; stretch: ask the student to write one more expression that equals 400.

items.prompt: On a number grid that runs from 451 to 530, each row has 10 numbers. Starting at 467, you add 10. Which number do you land on?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 467 + 10 = 477. On the grid this means moving one row down from 467.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Adding 10 increases the tens digit by 1 and leaves the hundreds and ones digits unchanged.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student added 1 instead of 10, moving one cell to the right rather than one row down.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student added 20 instead of 10, moving two rows down.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student added 90 instead of 10, possibly confusing the number of columns in the grid.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student trace the move on the actual grid and count 10 cells; stretch: ask which number they land on if they then subtract 40 from 477.

items.prompt: Extend this chain: 312, ___, ___, 612. Each step adds the same amount. What is added each time?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The chain goes 312, 412, 512, 612 — each step adds 100. Only the hundreds digit changes.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Notice that only the hundreds digit changes across the chain; the step size must be 100.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student identified that the ones digit is unchanged but chose the smallest place-value unit.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student noticed a digit change but confused the hundreds column change with a tens-place operation.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student computed 612 − 312 = 300 and reported the total difference rather than the per-step amount.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write all four numbers and underline the hundreds digit in each, asking which digit changes; stretch: ask the student to continue the chain two more steps and name the next two numbers.

exercise.description: Extend two chains: Add 100 repeatedly from 269; Add 10 repeatedly from 269; Add 1 repeatedly from 269; repeat for 454.

items.prompt: A number web has 130 in the centre. One path adds 7 to reach a neighbour; another path subtracts 3 to reach a different neighbour. Write the two neighbours of 130 in this web.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply each operation (+7 and −3) directly to the centre number to find the connected neighbours.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student count on or back on a number line from 130; stretch: ask the student to find what number, when connected to 130 by a +7 step, would itself connect to 156 by another +7 step.

exercise.description: Fill in boxes in the number web connecting 120 and 130 via +3/−3/+7/−7 operations, extending to 156 and 175.

items.prompt: A farmer packed 320 saplings in the morning. By evening, 84 saplings had been sold. How many saplings are left? Draw a box diagram with the two numbers before you calculate.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Exchange 1 ten for 10 ones (since the ones column has 0), then subtract 4 ones; exchange 1 hundred for 10 tens, then subtract 8 tens; subtract hundreds.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: provide an HTO table and let the student draw block pictures for 320 before crossing out 84; stretch: ask how many more saplings need to be sold for the farmer to have fewer than 200 left.

exercise.description: Draw box diagrams and use HTO blocks or number line to solve: (1) 456−63; (2) 309+80; (3) 270−36.

items.section_title: Indian currency: notes, coins, and equivalence
items.prompt: Sunita wants to buy a book that costs ₹45. She has one ₹50 note. Show two different ways she could pay exactly ₹45 using the notes and coins she might get as change or already have: one way using a ₹20 note and some coins, and one way using only ₹10 notes and coins.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Way 1: one ₹20 note + two ₹10 notes + one ₹5 coin = ₹20 + ₹20 + ₹5 = ₹45. Alternatively: one ₹20 note + one ₹10 note + three ₹5 coins = ₹45. Way 2: four ₹10 notes + one ₹5 coin = ₹40 + ₹5 = ₹45.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Combine available denominations so that the notes and coins total the given price, trying different groupings.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: lay out play notes and coins and physically arrange them to total ₹45; stretch: ask the student to find a third way to make ₹45 using only ₹5 and ₹10 denominations.

exercise.description: Use given notes and coins to buy items priced ₹55, ₹30, ₹28, ₹20; find at least two ways of making each amount.

items.prompt: Rekha saves ₹125 every month. After 3 months she spends ₹200 on books. How much money does she have left?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add ₹125 three times to find the total saved, then subtract ₹200 from the total.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw three boxes each labelled ₹125 and add them in two steps (125+125=250, then 250+125=375); stretch: ask how many more months Rekha needs to save to buy something costing ₹500.

exercise.description: Solve using box diagrams and notes or number line: (1) ₹650+₹250; (2) ₹500−₹209; (3) ₹150+₹100×4 weeks; (4) ₹250+₹125+₹350.

items.section_title: Number card game and computation drill
items.prompt: Solve: 600 − 82 = ___. Show your working in an HTO table.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Exchange 1 hundred for 10 tens, then 1 ten for 10 ones; subtract 2 ones and 8 tens; the hundreds column becomes 5.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw the HTO table and write 6, 0, 0 in the three columns; let the student use block pictures to show the exchange before writing the digits; stretch: ask the student to also solve 700 − 82 and compare the two answers.
